![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14253560/assets/39f62ad81b496c06c2e89ee01110ca2ad1873512056f50daf13348d3906a05c9.png)

The diagram above shows the unit circle. Given that $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2},$ what is the value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ?$
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14253560/assets/f90e6b431e9371bd01250b3c2a5033e2556e9f4d99d2a171f658785276cf00b5.png)

We can use the Pythagorean identity to find $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta :$

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1 \\ {sin}^{2}⁡\theta  & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & =\pm \sqrt{1-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{1-\frac{1}{4}} \\  & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\pm \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We select the negative answer since $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $ is negative in the fourth quadrant. So, $\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.$
